summaries.example: Imagine a note that says “homework” three times and “remember” once. There are four word tokens: four particular marks or sounds. But there are only two word types: the different words being used, “homework” and “remember.” The same idea works for three cars of the same model: three cars are tokens, while the shared model is one type.
summaries.summary: The type/token distinction helps explain why two different counts can both be right. A page may contain many particular marks of a word, but only one different word. The particular marks, sounds, performances, or mental occurrences are tokens. The repeatable word, song, or pattern is a type. A type can have many tokens, and sometimes philosophers wonder whether it could have only one or none. The distinction is useful for words, repeatable artworks, and mental states such as pain. It also raises deeper questions: Do types exist? Are they abstract? Which things can be types? Philosophers do not agree on all the answers. Some think types are abstract things; others think words or artworks may be different kinds of things, even if they are not types.
key_ideas: One word can mean either a general word type or one particular word token.
Types can have many tokens, such as many written uses of one word or many performances of one song.
The difference helps us count things in more than one correct way.
Philosophers ask whether types really exist and what kinds of things can be types.
summaries.why_it_matters: This distinction prevents confusion. For example, a teacher may ask how many words appear on a page and mean either different words or individual uses. Philosophers also use the distinction when thinking about songs, artworks, minds, and physical events. It shows that counting and talking about “the same thing” can depend on whether we mean a repeatable pattern or one particular occurrence.

important_terms.definition: A particular thing, event, mark, sound, or occurrence that happens in a specific place or time.
A repeatable kind or pattern that can have many particular examples or occurrences.
A particular occurrence of a type. For example, one written use of a word can be an instance of that word.
Something not located in one particular place or time, such as the word or song considered apart from its individual uses or performances.

questions_to_think_about: If a song is never performed, could it still be a song type?
Is a word the same thing as any one mark or sound used to show it?
When you count books, are you counting copies, kinds of books, or both?
Can one thing belong to more than one type?

summaries.example: Suppose a page contains fifty inscriptions of “the.” It is true that there are fifty word tokens on the page, but it may also be true that only one word type occurs there. The type/token distinction explains the two readings without treating them as a simple mistake. A similar contrast appears between a song and its performances: a particular concert performance is a token, while the repeatable musical work may be treated as a type.
summaries.summary: The entry examines a distinction introduced by C. S. Peirce and later applied far beyond words. A token is a particular occurrence, such as one inscription, utterance, performance, or particular instance of pain. A type is the repeatable entity that tokens may instantiate, such as a word, a musical work, or a mental-state pattern. The distinction explains why “there are two words” and “there are four words” can both be correct when a note contains repeated uses: one count concerns types, the other tokens. The philosophical difficulty begins when we ask what types and tokens are. Familiar tokens are often concrete particulars, but examples involving spaces, absences, numbers, or properties resist a single simple definition. Types are commonly treated as abstract, yet some seem to have histories or properties that ordinary abstract objects do not. The entry considers three arguments for types: certain counting claims seem to need a type as their truth-maker; many true sentences appear to refer directly to types; and ordinary language talks about types and kinds. Each argument can be challenged by paraphrase, alternative ontologies, or doubts about whether the relevant non-token is really a type. Further questions concern whether all types have tokens, whether the type/token relation is one relation or a family of related relations, and how knowledge of types can be gained through contact with tokens. The distinction may also differ from the relations between sets and members, universals and particulars, or kinds and instances.
key_ideas: The same expression can support type-level and token-level readings, so counting alone can reveal an important metaphysical distinction.
Tokens are often concrete particulars, but unusual cases involving spaces, absences, numbers, or properties complicate simple definitions.
Arguments for types appeal to counting claims, truths apparently about types, and ordinary talk about kinds or types.
Whether types exist is disputed: some views accept them, while others paraphrase type-talk or posit non-token entities that are not types.
Types are often called abstract, but their apparent histories, properties, and relations to tokens create pressure for more qualified accounts.
The type/token relation may not be uniform across words, artworks, and mental states; even knowledge of types may arise through different routes.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction clarifies debates in metaphysics, philosophy of language, aesthetics, and philosophy of mind. It helps separate a repeatable word from its written or spoken occurrences, a musical work from its performances, and a mental-state type from particular episodes. Without this separation, claims about identity, counting, existence, and knowledge can become ambiguous. At the same time, the entry shows that the distinction is not automatically a complete theory: philosophers still need to explain what types are, which entities qualify, and how types relate to their tokens.

important_terms.definition: A particular occurrence of something, usually located in space and time, such as an inscription, utterance, performance, or particular mental occurrence.
A repeatable entity or pattern that may have one, many, or possibly no tokens. Words and repeatable artworks are standard examples discussed in the entry.
The relation in which a particular occurrence counts as an occurrence of a repeatable entity or pattern.
An entity understood as lacking ordinary spatial or temporal location. Types are often treated this way, although that view is debated.
The view that claims apparently about types can be analyzed as claims about tokens, without commitment to types as entities.
A non-token entity that makes a true claim true. Counting arguments ask whether a type is needed as the witness for claims such as “there is one word on the page.”
A general category whose members or instances share some relevant basis. Kinds may overlap with types, but the relationship is not settled.
A property or relation understood as capable of having instances. Some philosophers compare types with universals, while also noting important differences.

questions_to_think_about: Does the truth of “the is the most common word in English” require a word type, or can it be paraphrased entirely in terms of tokens?
Could a newly composed song be a type before anyone performs it? What would count as its first token?
If an inscription has the same shape in English and French, what makes it a token of one word rather than the other?
Are types best understood as abstract entities, kinds, universals, or something else?
Can one general type/token relation explain both a song and its performances and a mental state such as pain and its particular occurrences?

summaries.example: A music club performs the same song three times. You can say, “Three songs were performed” if you mean three performances, or “One song was performed” if you mean one different musical work. The performances are tokens. The repeatable song is a type. The two answers count different things, so both can make sense.
summaries.summary: The type/token distinction separates a repeatable thing from one of its particular occurrences. For example, three performances can be tokens of one song type, just as several inscriptions can be tokens of one word type. This distinction explains why a person can correctly give two different counts for the same situation. The entry asks whether types really exist, what sorts of things they are, and whether they are abstract. One argument begins with counting: if it is true that one word appears on a page even though there are many inscriptions, perhaps a type is needed to make that claim true. Another argument points to sentences such as “The is the most frequently used word,” which seem to be about a word type, not one inscription. A third argument comes from ordinary phrases such as “a type of animal,” although ordinary uses of “type” do not always match philosophers’ uses of the term. Critics may try to explain type-level sentences as generalizations about tokens, or they may accept words and artworks while denying that these are types. The entry also considers whether tokens must be concrete particulars, whether types can exist without tokens, and whether the relation between a type and its tokens is always the same. It compares the distinction with related ideas such as kinds and instances, sets and members, and universals and particulars. The overall lesson is that the distinction is useful but philosophically unsettled.
key_ideas: Types and tokens give us two ways to count the same situation.
A token is usually a particular occurrence; a type can be repeated in many occurrences.
Words, repeatable artworks, and mental states are important examples in the philosophical discussion.
Some arguments say types must exist because ordinary counting and true sentences seem to refer to them.
Other philosophers try to explain these sentences using only tokens or by accepting non-token things that are not types.
There is no settled answer about whether types are abstract or whether one single type/token relation fits every case.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many disagreements become clearer when we ask whether they concern a general repeatable entity or a particular occurrence. This matters when discussing language, music, art, and the mind. It also teaches a broader philosophical habit: do not assume that an everyday word has only one meaning or that one correct count must replace all others. Different answers may reflect different objects being counted. Understanding that difference helps us evaluate competing theories rather than arguing past one another.

important_terms.definition: One particular occurrence, such as one written word, spoken word, song performance, or episode of pain.
A repeatable kind of thing that can appear in many particular occurrences, such as a word or song.
A particular occurrence that belongs to a type. A performance can be an instance of a song.
A thing considered apart from any one location or time. Philosophers often describe types this way, but they debate whether all types are abstract.
A claim about a repeatable thing rather than one particular occurrence, such as “this song is three minutes long.”
A category or kind. Some philosophers think kinds and types are closely related, while others think the words do not line up perfectly.

questions_to_think_about: If three people write the same word, are there three words, one word, or both?
Can something be a type even if it has never had a token?
Why might a performance be a token of a song even when it is played badly?
Are a word and its type the same thing?
Do mental states work exactly like words and songs in the type/token distinction?
